title: Nuclear Fission and Fusion
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Splitting and Joining for Energy

Both routes to nuclear energy walk up the binding-energy curve toward iron: **fission** splits a heavy nucleus, **fusion** joins light ones. Each gram of fuel converts milligrams of mass into energy millions of times beyond any chemical reaction.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2022)

### 2.1 Nuclear fission

A heavy nucleus (A > 200) absorbs a neutron and splits into two medium nuclei plus neutrons and energy:
$$^{235}_{92}U + n \rightarrow ^{141}_{56}Ba + ^{92}_{36}Kr + 3n + \text{energy}$$
- The fragments have higher BE/A than uranium — the mass difference appears as ~200 MeV per fission.
- Released neutrons can trigger further fissions: a **chain reaction** (controlled in reactors via moderators and control rods; uncontrolled in weapons).
- Used in nuclear reactors.

### 2.2 Nuclear fusion

Two light nuclei merge into a heavier one, releasing energy:
$$^{2}_{1}H + ^{3}_{1}H \rightarrow ^{4}_{2}He + n + 17.6 \text{ MeV}$$
- Requires enormous temperature (~10⁸ K) to overcome Coulomb repulsion — hence "thermonuclear".
- Powers the Sun and stars; the goal of fusion reactors (plasma confinement). Per kilogram, fusion releases more energy than fission.

### 2.3 Why both release energy (NEB 2022, 3m)

The BE/A curve peaks at iron-56. Heavy nuclei fission and light nuclei fuse — each move **toward the iron peak raises BE/A**, and the increase times the nucleon count is the energy released, supplied by the corresponding mass loss (Δm c²).

### 2.4 Comparison (NEB 2022, 3m)

| | Fission | Fusion |
|---|---|---|
| Process | Heavy nucleus splits | Light nuclei combine |
| Example | ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n | ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n |
| Conditions | Neutron capture; possible at room T | ~10⁸ K (thermonuclear) |
| Energy per event | ~200 MeV | 17.6 MeV (but higher per kg) |
| By-products | Radioactive waste | Mostly harmless helium |
| Application | Reactors | Stars; experimental reactors |

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 109:** the BE/A curve is the master explanation of both processes.
- **To Topic 108:** the released energy equals the mass loss × c².
- **To Topic 107:** fission fragments are radioactive isotopes with their own half-lives.

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

1. Explain the chain reaction and reactor control (3m).
2. Mass-to-energy numerical for a fission event (3m).
3. Why does the Sun need fusion, not fission? (2m)

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Forgetting the example equations — they carry marks in the 3m comparison.
2. Saying fusion happens "at room temperature" — the Coulomb barrier demands ~10⁸ K.
3. Claiming fission yields more energy *per kilogram* — fusion wins per kg, fission per event.
specificConditions: Criticality: Chain reaction self-sustains when each fission causes exactly one more fission (k = 1). k < 1 subcritical, k > 1 supercritical.
Fusion Temperature: ~10⁸ K needed — much hotter than sun's core (~1.5×10⁷ K) because terrestrial fusion uses D-T (easier than p-p).
Fissile vs Fertile: ²³⁵U, ²³³U, ²³⁹Pu are fissile (fission with thermal neutrons). ²³⁸U, ²³²Th are fertile (convert to fissile via neutron capture).

- ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + ~200 MeV
- ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV
- E = Δmc²

Fusion: light nuclei combine at ~10⁸ K, e.g. ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV. Both release energy as BE/A rises toward iron.

mcs.explanation: Fission = splitting of heavy nucleus into lighter fragments.

mcs.question: Energy released per ²³⁵U fission is approximately:
mcs.explanation: Typical fission releases ~200 MeV per nucleus.

mcs.question: Nuclear fusion requires:
mcs.explanation: ~10⁸ K to overcome Coulomb repulsion between nuclei.

mcs.explanation: Moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb excess neutrons.

mcs.explanation: Fusion converts ~0.4% mass vs fission ~0.1% — more energy per kg.

summary: **Fission** splits a heavy nucleus: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + ~200 MeV, with the freed neutrons sustaining a **chain reaction** (controlled in reactors by moderators and control rods). **Fusion** joins light nuclei: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV, but demands ~10⁸ K to overcome Coulomb repulsion — the engine of the Sun. Both release energy because the binding energy per nucleon rises toward iron-56 (NEB 2022, 3m); per kilogram fusion releases more energy and leaves only helium, while fission produces radioactive waste.

subtopics.name: Fission
points: A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei plus neutrons
Example: U-235 + n gives Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3n
Releases about 200 MeV per fission event

subtopics.name: Fusion
points: Two light nuclei combine into a heavier one
Example: four protons fuse to helium in the Sun
Releases more energy per unit mass than fission

subtopics.name: Chain reaction
points: Each fission releases neutrons that can trigger further fissions
Critical mass is the minimum mass needed to sustain the chain
Controlled in a reactor by moderators and control rods

subtopics.name: Fusion conditions
points: Requires extremely high temperature to overcome Coulomb repulsion
Requires high density and sufficient confinement time
Lawson criterion sets the threshold for net energy gain

subtopics.name: Energy comparison
points: Fusion releases about 4 times more energy per kilogram than fission
Fusion fuel (deuterium) is abundant in seawater
Fusion produces far less long-lived radioactive waste

subtopics.name: Practical status
points: Fission is commercially mature and supplies about 10% of world electricity
Fusion remains experimental; ITER is the flagship project
The Sun is the only proven sustained fusion reactor
